title: That we taste nothing pure
paragraphs: The feebleness of our condition is such that things cannot, in their natural simplicity and purity, fall into our use. The elements we enjoy are altered, and so it is with metals; gold must be debased with some other matter to fit it for our service. Neither has virtue, as simple as the one that Aristo, Pyrrho, and the Stoics made the end of life — nor the Cyrenaic and Aristippic pleasure — ever been useful to us without mixture. Of the pleasures and goods we enjoy, there is not one exempt from some mixture of evil and inconvenience:
"Medio de fonte leporum, Surgit amari aliquid, quod in ipsis floribus angat."
["From the very fountain of our pleasures, something bitter rises up, which torments us even among the flowers." — Lucretius, iv. 1130.]

Our keenest pleasure has some sort of groaning and complaining in it. Would you not say that it is dying of pain? In fact, when we frame the image of it in its full excellence, we stuff it with sickly and painful adjectives and qualities: languor, softness, feebleness, faintness, morbidezza — a great testimony of their consanguinity and consubstantiality. The deepest joy has more of severity than of cheer in it. The highest, fullest contentment offers more of gravity than of merriment:
"Ipsa felicitas, se nisi temperat, premit."
["Even happiness, unless it moderates itself, oppresses us." — Seneca, Ep., 74.]

Pleasure chews and grinds us. According to the old Greek line, which says that the gods sell us all the goods they give us — meaning that they give us nothing pure and perfect, and that we only buy at the price of some evil.

Labour and pleasure, very unlike in nature, are nevertheless joined together by I know not what natural junction. Socrates says that some god tried to blend and confound pain and pleasure into one mass, but, not being able to do it, contented himself with coupling them by the tail. Metrodorus said that in sorrow there is some mixture of pleasure. I do not know whether he meant anything else by that; but for my part, I am of the opinion that there is design, consent, and complacency in giving oneself up to melancholy. I say that besides ambition, which may also have a hand in the business, there is some shadow of delight and delicacy that smiles upon and flatters us even in the very lap of melancholy. Are there not some temperaments that feed on it?
"Est quaedam flere voluptas;"
["There is a certain kind of pleasure in weeping." — Ovid, Trist., iv. 3, 27.]
and one Attalus in Seneca says that the memory of friends we have lost is as pleasing to us as bitterness is to the palate in wine that is too old:
"Minister vetuli, puer, Falerni Inger' mi calices amariores" —
["Boy, when you pour out the old Falernian, pour the bitterest into my bowl." — Catullus, xxvii. 1.]
and as apples that have a sweet tartness.

Nature shows us this confusion. Painters hold that the same motions and contortions of the face that serve for weeping serve also for laughter; and indeed, before either is finished, just watch the painter's handling and you will be in doubt as to which of the two the design tends. The extreme of laughter ends in tears:
"Nullum sine auctoramento malum est."
["No evil is without its compensation." — Seneca, Ep., 69.]

When I imagine a man laden with all the conveniences anyone could desire — let us suppose that all his members were always seized by a pleasure like that of generation, in its most excessive height — I feel him melting under the weight of his delight, and see him utterly unable to bear so pure, so continual, and so universal a pleasure. Indeed, he is running away while he is there, and naturally hurries to escape, as from a place where he cannot stand firm, and where he is afraid of sinking.

When I religiously confess myself to myself, I find that the best virtue I have has in it some tincture of vice; and I am afraid that Plato, in his purest virtue (I, who am as sincere and loyal a lover of virtue of that stamp as anyone) — if he had listened and put his ear close to himself, and he did so, no doubt — would have heard some jarring note of human mixture, but faint, and perceptible only to himself. Man is wholly and throughout but patch and motley. Even the laws of justice themselves cannot subsist without some mixture of injustice; so much so that Plato says they undertake to cut off the hydra's head who pretend to clear the law of all inconveniences:
"Omne magnum exemplum habet aliquid ex iniquo, quod contra singulos utilitate publics rependitur,"
["Every great example has in it some mixture of injustice, which is set against the wrong done to particular men by the public good it brings." — Tacitus, Annals, xiv. 44.]
says Tacitus.

It is likewise true that for the use of life and the service of public commerce, there can be some excesses in the purity and sharpness of our minds; that penetrating light has in it too much of subtlety and curiosity. We must dull and blunt them a little, to make them more obedient to example and practice, and veil and obscure them somewhat, the better to suit them to this dark and earthly life. So common and less speculative souls are found more apt for, and more successful in, the management of affairs; and the elevated and exquisite opinions of philosophy are unfit for business. This sharp vivacity of soul, and the supple, restless quickness that goes with it, disturb our negotiations. We need to handle human enterprises more superficially and roughly, and leave a great part to fortune; it is not necessary to examine affairs with so much subtlety and so deep — a man loses himself in considering so many contrary lustres, so many various forms:
"Volutantibus res inter se pugnantes, obtorpuerunt.... animi."
["While they were considering things at variance with each other, their minds were stunned and they knew not what to do." — Livy, xxxii. 20.]

It is what the ancients say of Simonides: that because his imagination, when King Hiero put a question to him (to answer which he had been given many days for thought), suggested to him so many sharp and subtle considerations, while he was doubting which was the most likely, he despaired of the truth altogether.

The man who dives into a question and in his inquiry takes in all the circumstances and consequences, hinders his own choice. A small engine well handled is enough for executions, whether of less or greater weight. The best managers are those who can least give an account of how they are so; while the greatest talkers, for the most part, do nothing to the purpose. I know one of this sort of men, an excellent discourser on every kind of good husbandry, who has miserably let a hundred thousand livres of yearly revenue slip through his hands; I know another who talks, who better advises than anyone of his council, and there is not in the world a finer show of soul and understanding than he makes; and yet when he comes to the test, his servants find him quite another thing — not to mention his misfortunes.
